---
title: "Disrupt-Potentiate-Rewire-Homeostasis (DPRH)"
author: "Anselm Jeong"
date: "2026-01-26"
bibliography: "Metaplasticity.bib"
---

Drawing on insights from the therapeutic mechanisms of psychedelics, we can now propose a model that characterizes the relationships between different plasticity-enhancing treatments. We have seen that psychedelics first induce widespread network desynchronization to create a state of "chaos," followed by an enhanced neuroplastic window that enables network reconfiguration or the remodeling of the attractor landscape. This motif can be applied to ECT and other treatments.

ECT induces controlled seizures that trigger extensive neurophysiological changes (10.1038/s41386-023-01677-2). Unlike pharmacological interventions that gradually modulate synaptic function, ECT causes a transient, non-specific, and large-scale neural disruption. Functional neuroimaging studies show that ECT induces consistent changes in large-scale connectivity patterns, including the Default Mode Network (DMN), Salience Network (SN), and Fronto-Parietal Control Network (FPCN) (10.1038/tp.2014.124; 10.1038/s41398-020-00961-9; 10.1073/pnas.1117206109). Specifically, it is associated with reduced pathological hyperconnectivity, normalization of aberrant network interactions, and increased variability and flexibility in functional connectivity. The breadth of these changes suggests that ECT expands the dynamic range of the system's accessible state space rather than selectively normalizing specific pathological circuits (10.1038/s41380-023-02015-0). This process closely resembles the widespread desynchronization induced by psychedelics.

Notably, the extensive network changes induced by ECT overlap temporally with a window of significantly increased neuroplasticity. While the causal sequence—whether neurophysiological changes first drive FC changes and subsequently induce SC changes, or neuroplasticity-induced SC changes lead to altered FC—remains a subject of debate, the motif of network disruption followed by an opportunity for remodeling is consistent. Furthermore, just as psychedelic therapy requires subsequent psychotherapy to be effective, the clinical effects of ECT are often difficult to sustain without maintenance pharmacotherapy.

As we will see, this common motif also applies to pharmacotherapy and rTMS, with slight variations. In the case of ECT, Ousdal et al. (10.1016/j.biopsych.2021.05.023) formalized this sequence as a three-stage process: "disrupt–potentiate–rewire." First, intense generalized seizures cause an immediate disruption that resets the rigid, pathological patterns of the neural network. Second, in response to this disruption, surges in growth factors such as BDNF potentiate neuroplastic changes. Finally, within this highly plastic window, interactions with therapeutic environments rewire the brain into more healthy configurations. They also noted that this sequence is inherently neutral—a double-edged sword that can lead to either therapeutic transformation or confusing chaos. Thus, ECT does not cure depression simply by inducing the growth of new neurons or synaptic connections; rather, it acts as a controlled biological stressor that initiates the "disrupt–potentiate–rewire" sequence. 

This perspective aligns with the "iPlasticity" (induced plasticity) model proposed by Eero Castrén (10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2013.1; 10.1016/j.tins.2013.01.005). He argued that antidepressants do not merely correct a chemical imbalance but rather reopen a flexible "critical period" akin to that of the juvenile brain. In this model, pharmacological agents provide an opportunity for change, while the specific direction of healthy circuit rewiring is determined by subsequent environmental input and psychotherapeutic intervention. Both the disrupt–potentiate–rewire sequence and iPlasticity framework underscore that potentiated neuroplasticity may remain unstable or even maladaptive without appropriate ongoing therapeutic guidance.

Building on these frameworks, we propose that an additional stage is necessary to maintain remission and prevent relapse. A sustained state of heightened plasticity implies that the brain remains vulnerable to returning to previous maladaptive patterns. Even if therapists facilitate long-term rewiring through intensive interventions, such treatment efforts cannot be maintained indefinitely. Ultimately, the brain must regain the capacity to maintain a healthy network organization. This capacity is governed by metaplasticity, specifically homeostatic plasticity, which regulates the brain's plastic potential. It is the mechanism that determines when to open a window for reconfiguration and when to close it to preserve stability. While it remains unclear which specific treatments effectively target homeostatic plasticity, we argue that it is another critical component of the whole recovery process. Therefore, we propose extending the sequence described by Ousdal et al. by adding a final stage, resulting in the "disrupt–potentiate–rewire–homeostasis" (DPRH) model.

참고자료



결국 가소성의 증가로 을 증진함으로써 경직된 네트워크를 이완시키고, 병적 상태를 유지하던 제약을 완화할 수 있다. 끌개 분지(attractor basin) 관점에서 보면, ECT는 뇌의 에너지 지형을 평탄화하여 끌개의 안정성을 감소시키는 것으로 해석할 수 있다(10.1155/2015/271674; 10.1002/hbm.23928).

신경생물학적 수준에서 ECT는 BDNF, 혈관내피성장인자, 특히 해마의 시냅스생성 및 신경생성 마커를 포함한 가소성 관련 인자를 강력하게 상향조절한다(10.1016/j.jpsychires.2016.08.004; 10.1111/acps.13080). 동물 모델에서도 전기경련 자극은 새로운 시냅스, 뉴런, 신경교세포, 혈관의 생성을 유도하며, BDNF를 비롯한 영양인자의 발현을 증가시킨다. 이러한 세포 수준의 가소성 변화는 거시적 수준의 MRI 연구 결과와도 일치한다.



이러한 효과는 단순한 가소성 증진을 넘어, 가소적 변화를 지배하는 *규칙* 자체의 변화—즉 후속 학습과 적응의 역치를 낮추는 메타가소성 조절—을 반영하는 것으로 볼 수 있다(10.1038/s41380-022-01746-w).
